text: You get an array called candidates, of distinct integers, and a target. Return all unique combinations that sum to target. You may use the same number as many times as you want. Any order is fine.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — two, two, three and two, three, two are the same combination, so I return it only once. A number can repeat, but two combinations are different only if the counts differ. Is that right? And if no combination works, I return an empty list.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and thirty. Each candidate is between two and forty, all distinct, and the target is between one and forty. Tests guarantee fewer than 150 combinations.

Okay. Every value is at least two, so a sum only goes up as I add numbers. Once I pass the target, that branch is dead. Let me run through the example. Two, three, six, seven with target seven gives two, two, three, and seven alone. Two, three, five with target eight gives four twos, two, three, three, and three, five. And just two with target one gives an empty list.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try every count for every candidate — zero copies, one copy, two copies, and so on — then check the sum. That works, and I'll use it later as a checker, but it builds a lot of dead branches. This problem reminds me of the backtracking template for building subsets with a start index, where each level only picks from position s onward. There are two changes. A number can be reused, so I recurse with i, not i plus one. And I stop a branch as soon as the sum is too big.

Here's the plan. One: sort the candidates. Two: in the search, if the sum equals target, record the path. Three: loop i from s; if adding candidates at i passes the target, break; otherwise push, recurse with i, and pop. I'm using s to keep track of where I may start picking, so every combination is built in non-decreasing index order — two, three can appear, but three, two never does. One thing worth flagging — the recursive call passes i, so I may pick the same number again. With i plus one, two with target four would give nothing instead of two, two. There's a trade-off here. I pay for a sort, and in return, once one candidate is too big, every later one is too, so I break the whole loop. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. The main function sorts, then starts the search with an empty path, sum zero, and start zero. The search records the path when the sum hits target; otherwise it loops from s, pushes, recurses with i, and pops. One thing worth flagging — the break is only safe because of the sort. It's a correctness point, not just speed. If I drop the sort and keep the break, three, two with target two gives nothing: the loop sees three, breaks, and never looks at two. Also, I never call the search with a sum over target, because I check before I push. So there's no sum-over-target base case.
Would continue work instead of break? And path is passed by value. Is that OK?

Let me walk through that. Yes, continue is still correct. It makes the same calls, because every skipped candidate would fail the check anyway — but it keeps looping over them. On a stress test, candidates two through thirty-one with target forty, there are 6,131 answers, and both make 37,271 calls. Break runs 68,380 loop iterations; continue runs 635,407. By value is correct too. Each call gets its own copy, and the pop back still undoes the push inside that call. But every call pays for a copy. By reference, there's one shared path, and the push and pop pair keeps it clean. Same calls, same answers — on that stress test, 0.41 milliseconds versus 1.29 by value.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Two, three, six, seven with target seven, expected two, two, three and seven. The row that matters is call five. Back in call three, the loop moves on to i equals one and pushes three, so the child starts at s equals one and can never pick a two again. That's why two, three, two never shows up. Every other branch breaks the moment its sum passes seven. Ten calls in total, and the result matches. Corner cases: two with target one returns empty in one call. Recursing with i plus one makes two with target four return empty. Recursing with s, or starting at zero, makes two, three with target five return both orders. No sort but keeping the break makes three, two with target two return empty. I also compared against the count-every-copy version on 3,024 small cases: zero wrong.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is exponential, bounded by the size of the search tree. With N candidates, target T, and smallest candidate M, a path is at most T over M deep, with at most N choices per level, so a rough bound is N to the power T over M, plus the sort and copying each answer. Space is T over M extra for the recursion stack and the path, not counting the output; by value, each level also holds its own copy. On the stress test, far past the 150-answer guarantee, that's 37,271 calls; without any pruning, 635,408. Oh, one more thing — the real bound is much smaller than N to the T over M. The pruning cuts every branch the moment it passes the target, so the tree is only as big as the sums that still fit.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw that recursing with i allows reuse and starting at s blocks duplicates, and you had two with target four, and two, three with target five, ready as proof. You knew the break depends on the sort, and showed that three, two with target two returns empty. And you measured the costs: break versus continue, by value versus by reference. Good work.
